lines.text: Mind your feet that side. There's hot scale down there and it goes through a boot sole.
If it's the warm floor you've come about, ask away, only ask me while I'm working. My father put my hand down flat on it when I was seven.
Put your hand flat on the floor. Go on — by the anvil, where the flagstone's worn smooth.
Warm, isn't it. And that's nothing off my forge, forge is cold till I light it after noon. Most people say vent, and a vent comes up hot for an hour and then it's finished with you.

This floor has never come up like that. The men underground call it the warm shell. Gerta has the third shaft eight degrees over the fourth, her figure and not mine. Go up to the shaft head and look at the shrine there.
You got up to the shrine, then. Next time, take a candle in close and look along an edge where a plate's chipped. They aren't cut stone, those plates. They're shell.
I had a broken piece of one on this bench a month and put a chisel to it most days. Never marked it. Ask Gerta at the third shaft head for her log.
Right. So you got down to the deep shrine.
Kilnback. That's the word cut on the deep shrine, in the old letters. Somebody went into that reach and cut a name into a plate wider across than my doors, a long while before my father's father.

I've stood on this floor my whole working life and I still can't tell you what makes it warm. Gerta's readings say the heat hasn't shifted since before the fourth shaft was cut, bar two winters. I said she had those two wrong. She hadn't.
Go down when the vents are quiet. Take something at home in water, or made out of rock — nothing else will take a fire. Mind the last ladder, third rung's split.
So one of yours has aged out. You'll have the relic on you — folk generally carry it about for months not knowing what it's for.

What it's for is this. I set it into a collar-piece, plain brass, and the young one that wears it carries a bit of what the old one had. A bit of it. I've had grown men argue with me about how big a bit.
Bring it here and I'll set it. It wants a day and a night to cool once it's in, so come back through the town tomorrow.
There you are. Collar's cooled through and the seat's tight. Get your thumb on the relic and try to shift it — you won't.
I've put the old one's name underneath, on the side that sits against the strap. I do that on all of them, and it's not on the bill, so don't ask me what it comes to.
Fifth shaft's open as of this spring. They don't open a shaft on a hope.

There's enough coming off the steppe now to keep a crew fed while they dig it. Cragmar are grazing the high scarp again. My brother's lad has gone on the new shaft, and my brother's wife has said four words to me all week.

Fourth shaft's boarded up now. It didn't fall in, mind — nothing wrong with the fourth that a week's work would put right. But there's been next to nothing off the steppe these two seasons, and somebody in an office signed a paper.
The third stays open. I said my piece up at the office and they left it open. My father worked the third. I'll be in it while I can stand up in it.
One reading a shift, off the wall of the third shaft. Thirty-one years of it now.

It was never anybody's job. The shift before mine kept saying the third was warmer than the fourth, and I wanted to know whether they had it right. Then a few winters went by and it seemed daft to stop.
Bram's sent you up for the log. Here — one reading a shift, all of them mine, off the wall and not out of the air. The air moves down there, and you'd get a different number every time a door opened.
Eight degrees over the fourth. Same depth, the two shafts, so the fourth is what I measure against — boards on it or not, I've a key.

Bram will tell you the eight has never moved. He has that off me and he has it wrong. It went to fourteen in two winters out of thirty-one, four days at a stretch, and each of those followed a summer with no vent flare at all.

Go down the warm reach yourself before you take the log back. There's a shrine at the bottom and it isn't like the ones at the shaft head. No number on it anywhere, and I'm poor at a thing with no number.
There's a survey wants doing up on the steppe and it's a day's work, so tell me no if you haven't got a day. I'm below all week.
Five I want numbers on, all up on Cinder Steppe. Ashvole, Cragmar, Pyrelisk, Stonewing, Carricrow. Carricrow won't settle anywhere for long, so you'll put the same bird down as two if you hurry.

And what's growing up there. Walk the west scarp and tell me how far up the green gets to now — against the old cairn will do. Give me animals and nothing growing and I'm guessing, and I'd sooner not put a guess in the log.

choices.text: I'll go up and walk the steppe.

lines.text: Start at the west scarp, then the vent line, then the low ground on your way back. That's the order I walked it, so your figures sit next to my old ones. And if the vent line is flaring, leave it and come back another day.
All right. It was a whole day I was asking for, and that's a lot to ask of somebody who's just walked in. Find me at the third shaft head if you get a day spare.
Carricrow first. They don't settle on ground that's had nothing die on it lately. When their figure comes in high I stop looking at the birds and look at the other four.

Then I work up from the bottom, and the bottom is what's growing. Ashvole and Cragmar graze it. Pyrelisk take both, and Stonewing take Pyrelisk and nothing else up there. So if the green goes off that scarp, it comes up through the lot of them in order.
Your five go in beside my old ones tonight, in the back of the log where the pages have gone greasy off the lamp.
